COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Doctor — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace DOCTOR, match the doctor to the stethoscope, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the medicine bottles and draw one way you care for your body.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

← ScientistPrevious activityFirefighter →Next activity
HOW TO DO IT

Five little steps.

  1. 1

    Trace

    Trace the big dotted word DOCTOR letter by letter — say each letter’s name out loud as you go.

  2. 2

    Match

    Draw a line from the doctor to each of his three tools: the stethoscope, the bandage and the thermometer.

  3. 3

    Circle

    Six pictures sit in the grid — circle every one that shows a healthy habit. Look closely: not all six are healthy!

  4. 4

    Count

    Count the orange medicine bottles, then write the number in the box below them.

  5. 5

    Draw

    In the big empty box, draw one thing YOU do to take care of your body — brushing teeth, running, sleeping, anything true.

Ask a grown-up to read the steps aloud the first time. After that, you know just what to do.

YOUR PENCIL CASE

Pick your tools.

Pencil, nine crayons, an eraser, undo, redo and clear — the tools appear right here and work on the sheet. Save keeps your finished work as a picture, and your saved work comes back next time.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a doctor’s tools are for, which everyday habits keep bodies healthy, and how to read and write the word DOCTOR.

Knowledge to have ready: Your child needs a little vocabulary first: a doctor helps sick and hurt people, a stethoscope listens to heartbeats, a bandage protects a healing cut, and a thermometer checks temperature. Say each tool’s name before the pencil starts.

Why this activity matters: Doctors become familiar instead of frightening when children meet their tools on paper first. The healthy-habit grid also turns the worksheet into a gentle health talk, and the tracing row builds the same pre-writing muscles the alphabet class uses.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-habit awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing from life

What to say before you start: "This is a doctor — his tools help him take care of people. Trace his name, then find the three tools that belong with him. Now look at the six pictures: which ones show something healthy? Count the bottles slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing how YOU keep your body strong."

What to look for on the sheet: Point at the big picture together: the doctor wears a white coat and a blue tie and a stethoscope around his neck. In the match row, ask which tool would listen to a heartbeat. In the grid, ask your child to explain WHY a picture is or is not a healthy habit.

Questions to ask along the way: "Which doctor’s tool listens to your heart?" "Why do we wash hands before seeing the doctor?" "Which of the six habits do you do every day?" "What number did the medicine bottles count up to?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If a match line is hard, name the tools first and ask what each one touches. In the circle row, the tricky tiles are the ones that look fun — ask "does this help your body or just feel fun right now?" Count the bottles with one touch per bottle so the count stays honest.

Parent tips: Keep doctor talk friendly and honest — doctors help, and saying how you feel to a doctor is always allowed. Let your child own the pencil: the tracing can be wobbly and the drawing messy; the thinking is the work.

Understanding check: Ask: "Which tool listens to the heart? Name one healthy habit from the grid. How many bottles?" Right tool, one habit, the right count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Walk the healthy-habit grid at home today: the apple at snack time, the teeth brushing tonight, the running in the yard. Real repetition is what turns a circled picture into a habit.
